alt: A polythene rod rubbed with a cloth gains electrons from the cloth, so the rod becomes negative and the cloth positive. An acetate rod rubbed with a cloth loses electrons to the cloth, so the rod becomes positive and the cloth negative.
caption: Gain electrons: negative. Lose electrons: positive. Only electrons move.

alt: A rubbed polythene rod hangs in a paper stirrup. Bringing a second rubbed polythene rod near one end makes it turn away; bringing a rubbed acetate rod near makes it turn towards the acetate.
caption: Polythene repels polythene but attracts acetate, so the two gain opposite charges.

alt: A negatively charged balloon near a neutral wall. Electrons in the wall surface are repelled slightly away, leaving the nearby surface slightly positive. The pull from the near positive region is bigger than the push from the further negative region.
caption: A charged object attracts a neutral one because the nearer opposite charge wins.

alt: Three examples set out in three steps. Brushing hair transfers electrons so strands gain the same charge and repel. Walking on a nylon carpet charges a person, and touching a metal handle lets electrons flow suddenly, giving a shock. Rubbing fabrics in a dryer gives opposite charges that attract.
caption: Rubbing transfers electrons; the charges produced cause attraction, repulsion or a discharge.

alt: Left: fuel flowing into an aircraft transfers electrons, charge builds up and a spark can ignite fuel vapour. Right: the aircraft is joined to earth by a conducting cable, so electrons flow continuously and no large charge builds up.
caption: Earthing lets electrons flow away continuously, so no spark can form near fuel vapour.

alt: Five steps. The drum is charged all over; light from white parts of the page removes charge there; oppositely charged toner sticks only to the charged areas; charged paper attracts the toner; heat melts the toner onto the paper.
caption: Toner sticks only where the drum is still charged, which is where the page was dark.

alt: Charged ink drops leave a nozzle and pass between a positive and a negative deflecting plate. Negative drops curve towards the positive plate; drops with a bigger charge are deflected further before reaching the paper.
caption: Bigger charge, bigger deflection: the plates steer each drop to its place on the paper.
